overview: This file brings together U.S. and British economic-intelligence documents on Japan’s wartime iron, steel, and precision-engineering capabilities from 1940 to 1942. A naval attaché report describes shortages of alloying metals and high-quality special steel, rising raw-material costs, subsidies, and conflict between the Japanese Army and industrial interests; a Commerce Department memorandum assesses Japan’s dependence on imported scrap and pig iron while arguing that substantial stockpiles could sustain steel production after U.S. export restrictions; and a British Ministry of Economic Warfare study concludes that Japan could probably manufacture enough ball bearings for immediate military needs, although metallurgical and machine-tool weaknesses would impair their quality.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on scarcity of special steel in Japan
subfiles.from: H. H. Smith-Hutton, U.S. Naval Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Navy Department, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Reports shortages of high-quality special steel and alloying metals and the Japanese Army’s efforts to impose greater control over the steel industry.
subfiles.summary: Naval attaché reports Japan's special-steel shortage stems from cut German/Swedish supplies and depleted alloys, forcing steel subsidies over Diet action; only 5 of 80 registered special-steel firms rate first class, 69 inferior, amid Army-industry conflict over prioritizing military producers.

subfiles.title: George Wythe’s informal transmittal of the Japanese steel memorandum
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits informally a Commerce Department memorandum on raw materials for the Japanese steel industry.
subfiles.summary: Wythe informally forwards a Metals and Minerals Division memo on Japanese steel raw materials, at Assistant Director Wilson's request for Green's interest.

subfiles.title: Raw Material for the Japanese Steel Industry
subfiles.from: J. Jos. W. Palmer, Assistant Chief, Metals and Minerals Division
subfiles.about: Quantitatively evaluates Japan’s supply of scrap, pig iron, and iron ore and the likely effect of U.S. restrictions on scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum examines the effect of the October 1940 licensing restrictions that effectively ended U.S. scrap exports to Japan, using mostly 1934–1936 statistics because Japan had ceased publishing relevant figures after mid-1937. It reconstructs supplies from Japan, Korea, Manchuria, China, India, the Straits Settlements, and the United States, and estimates 1939 steel-ingot production at about six million tons. Palmer argues that imported American scrap was important but that Japan had probably accumulated between 1934 and 1939 at least 7.5 million tons of reserve pig iron and scrap, supplemented by material removed from occupied China. The memorandum concludes that these reserves, together with continuing supplies from Japan’s controlled territories, might sustain production at 1939 levels for at least one year and possibly two; tables compare world steel capacity and Japan’s raw-material balance in 1934–1936.

subfiles.title: London Embassy despatch transmitting memorandum on Japanese ball bearings
subfiles.from: James Somerville, for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy London
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: Transmits a British Ministry of Economic Warfare assessment of Japan’s capacity to replace foreign ball-bearing supplies with domestic production.
subfiles.summary: London Embassy forwards a British memo: four Japanese factories could make 60,000 bearings daily, likely enough in quantity but not quality, with existing good bearings in Japanese weapons likely prewar foreign stock, and interest in German bearings via blockade-running.

subfiles.title: Ministry of Economic Warfare memorandum on ball-bearing production in Japan
subfiles.from: Enemy Resources Department, Ministry of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Assesses the capacity, organization, technological limits, and probable product quality of Japan’s domestic ball-bearing industry.
subfiles.summary: British memo names four Japanese bearing makers with combined 60,000-bearing daily capacity (versus Germany's 220,000), probably sufficient quantitatively but limited by scarce grinding machinery and heat-treatment skill, expecting inferior quality versus Swedish imports.

interest: Shows Allied intelligence debating Japan's special-steel shortage, ferrous reserves, and ball-bearing quantity versus quality.
